text: Wells wrote the preface.

The exclusion, she wrote, had created, literally and figuratively, a White City, in the building of which the Colored American was allowed no helping hand, and in its glorious success he had no share.
They printed the pamphlet in several languages, so foreign visitors could read it.
Douglass had a base for the work.
He was serving as a commissioner for the Republic of Haiti, and Haiti had its own building at the fair.
He gave Wells a desk inside it.
Day after day, the two of them handed the pamphlet to passing visitors, many of them from abroad.
By the end, ten thousand copies were out, and Wells later said the message had reached far more people than that.
There was one day the fair set aside for Black Americans, the twenty-fifth of August.
The organizers called it Colored American Day.
Wells wanted nothing to do with it.
She saw it as a token, and she was furious at reports that officials meant to draw a crowd with free watermelon.
She stayed away.
Douglass went.
He was in his seventies by then, and when he rose to speak, hecklers in the crowd jeered at him about the Negro problem.
He set his prepared pages down.
He told them there was no Negro problem.
The real problem, he said, was whether the American people had loyalty enough, and honor enough, to live up to their own Constitution.
The young poet Paul Laurence Dunbar, who was working at the fair as a washroom attendant, read his verse that day.
Wells went to hear what people were saying about it, and she came away moved.
She later told Douglass that her youth had made her overreact.
The day had not been a mockery after all.
